title: The Ordinary Postcards
premise: August Crane, a literary translator whose childhood language is slipping away word by word, returns to her estranged family's coastal town for her grandmother's funeral. A stranger named Ivo recognizes the family by a name nobody uses — a name tied to a summer decades ago when the family sheltered a refugee boy who vanished, and to the debt they've been quietly repaying ever since. As August translates old letters and postcards sent but never delivered, she discovers that her own existence was part of the arrangement: a marriage of convenience meant to give the boy's daughter legitimacy. The question the whole family arranged itself around — what happened to the boy, Tomas — has an answer only her dying great-aunt can give, and August must reach her before silence does. In the end, August chooses to publish the translated letters under her real name, trading the family's careful anonymity for belonging on honest terms.
about_author: Paloma Ravensworth is the pen name of a former interpreter who spent a decade working between languages in border towns before turning to fiction. She writes about families that keep secrets the way other people keep heirlooms.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: August, POV: in her city apartment, she catalogs words from her childhood language she can no longer recall, a private ritual of loss. A phone call summons her to her grandmother's funeral. Beat: quiet grief for something not yet fully gone.

chapters.title: Salt and Lilies
chapters.summary: August, POV: the funeral in the coastal town is stiff with politeness; her mother performs grief, her father checks his watch. August feels like a guest at her own family's ceremony. Beat: alienation sharpened by ritual.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Knew
chapters.summary: August, POV: at the wake, a weathered stranger named Ivo greets the family by an unfamiliar surname. Her mother goes white; her father ushers him out. Ivo presses a postcard into August's hand as he leaves. Beat: first crack in the family's facade.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: August, POV: she confronts her mother about the name; her mother deflects with anger rather than denial. Great-aunt Vera, sharp-tongued and failing, watches from her chair and says only, 'Ask me while I still remember.' Beat: dread mixed with curiosity.

chapters.title: The Postcard
chapters.summary: August, POV: alone in her childhood bedroom, she studies the postcard — handwritten in her childhood language, addressed to a boy named Tomas, never stamped, never sent. The handwriting is her grandmother's. Beat: the past becomes physical.

chapters.title: Vera's Terms
chapters.summary: Vera, POV: the great-aunt agrees to talk, but only if August brings her the box of undelivered postcards locked in the attic. Vera's memory flickers between decades mid-sentence. Beat: bargaining with time itself.

chapters.title: The Attic Box
chapters.summary: August, POV: she finds the box — forty years of postcards, all written, none mailed, all in a language August half-remembers. Translating them will take everything she has left of it. Beat: inheritance as burden.

chapters.title: Summer of the Boy
chapters.summary: Vera, POV: the first true telling — 1979, a refugee boy washed ashore after a crossing gone wrong; the family hid him, gave him their unused second surname, taught him to be one of them. Beat: tenderness shadowed by fear.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: August, POV: translating the early postcards, she recovers words she thought lost — and learns Tomas wrote them himself in later years, from somewhere far away, asking questions the family never answered. Beat: language returning like a tide.

chapters.title: What Mother Knew
chapters.summary: Mother, POV: a flashback chapter — young and pregnant, she was persuaded into a marriage arranged so that Tomas's future child would have a legitimate name. She agreed because the family had saved her once too. Beat: sacrifice reframed as survival.

chapters.title: Ivo Returns
chapters.summary: August, POV: Ivo reappears — he was Tomas's friend from the camps, searching for him for decades. He believes Tomas came back to the town once, in winter, and was turned away. Beat: the family's kindness acquires a cruel edge.

chapters.title: The Winter Door
chapters.summary: Father, POV: he remembers the night someone knocked during a storm, and his own father ordered everyone silent behind the door — protecting the arrangement, or so he was told. He has carried the sound of knocking ever since. Beat: complicity confessed.

chapters.title: Postcards From the Middle Years
chapters.summary: August, POV: the middle postcards turn desperate — Tomas writing from hospitals, from detention, addressing each member of the family by name. One card is addressed to August herself, dated the year of her birth. Beat: rising urgency.

chapters.title: The Card With My Name
chapters.summary: August, POV: she translates it at last: 'If you are reading this, you are the reason they could keep pretending.' Shaken, she nearly burns it, then hides it instead. Beat: identity destabilized.

chapters.title: Vera Slips
chapters.summary: Vera, POV: Vera's memory collapses further; she confuses August with Tomas, speaks to her in the old language with heartbreaking fluency. August realizes Vera may hold the last living thread to what happened after the door. Beat: race against forgetting.

chapters.title: The Hospital Corridor
chapters.summary: August, POV: Vera is hospitalized; visiting hours become interrogations against time. A nurse mentions an old man used to visit every winter for years — always turned away at the house, always leaving postcards at the clinic. Beat: hope and horror entwined.

chapters.title: The Clinic Drawer
chapters.summary: August and Ivo, alternating POV: they find the clinic kept the postcards no one claimed — the final ones, including one saying Tomas was dying and asking only to see the sea once more. Beat: the question takes its final shape.

chapters.title: What Happened After the Door
chapters.summary: Vera, POV: lucid one last evening, Vera confesses: the family did open the door, eventually — two winters too late. They found nothing but footprints and a returned postcard. Whether Tomas lived, only the sea knows. Beat: climax of truth, anticlimax of certainty denied.

chapters.title: The Arrangement Undone
chapters.summary: August, POV: she lays the translated postcards before the assembled family. Her mother finally weeps; her father cannot speak. August asks the forbidden question aloud — why was I the price? — and receives, for the first time, an honest answer: fear, love, cowardice, all of it. Beat: catharsis through rupture.

chapters.title: Burial at the Tide Line
chapters.summary: August and Ivo, POV shared: they walk the shore where Tomas arrived, reading his last postcard aloud in the old language. August buries the unsent cards where the tide can take them — or return them. Beat: mourning without a grave.

chapters.title: Under My Own Name
chapters.summary: August, POV: back in the city, she finishes the translation and submits it for publication under her real name, refusing the family's old anonymity. Her mother sends a single line: 'Read it to me someday.' Beat: choosing honesty over inherited silence.

chapters.title: The First Sent Word
chapters.summary: August, POV: months later, holding the published book, she writes one final postcard — to Tomas, wherever he is — stamps it, and mails it to the sea. Some words, she understands now, are meant to travel even without an address. Beat: resolution; belonging found in the act of speaking.
